title: RCC structures-1
summary: Flexural design is the core, and three numbers do most of the work: 0.36 and 0.42 from the stress block, and x_u,max/d from the steel grade. The most examined concept is under-reinforced versus over-reinforced behaviour, and it is worth understanding rather than memorising — codes force under-reinforced design because steel yielding gives warning while concrete crushing does not. Development length and the minimum steel rules round out the subchapter and appear as one-line questions.

sections.heading: Assumptions and the stress block
sections.body:
**Assumptions for the limit state of collapse in flexure (IS 456 cl. 38.1):**

1. **Plane sections normal to the axis remain plane** after bending — so strain varies **linearly** with distance from the neutral axis.
2. The **maximum strain in concrete at the outermost compression fibre is 0.0035**.
3. The compressive stress–strain curve is **parabolic up to 0.002 strain, then constant** to 0.0035 (the rectangular-parabolic block), with a maximum stress of **0.67 f_ck/1.5 = 0.446 f_ck**.
4. The **tensile strength of concrete is IGNORED**.
5. Steel stress follows the design curve, with **maximum design stress 0.87 f_y**.
6. The **strain in tension steel at failure must be at least (0.87 f_y/E_s + 0.002)** — the ductility requirement.

Assumption 4 is worth pausing on: concrete's tensile strength is about a tenth of its compressive strength and is unreliable, so the whole tension zone below the neutral axis is taken as **cracked and carrying nothing**. All tension is carried by the steel. That single decision is what makes reinforced concrete design what it is.

Assumption 6 is the **ductility condition**, and it is the origin of the limiting neutral axis depth below.

**The stress block constants** — derived from the parabolic-rectangular shape, and both must be known:

> **Compressive force C = 0.36 f_ck b x_u**
> **Its centroid lies 0.42 x_u from the extreme compression fibre**

So **0.36** is the *area* coefficient of the stress block and **0.42** locates its *centroid*. The lever arm to the tension steel is therefore **(d − 0.42 x_u)**.

**Equilibrium and the neutral axis.** Setting C = T:

> **0.36 f_ck b x_u = 0.87 f_y A_st**
> **x_u = 0.87 f_y A_st / (0.36 f_ck b)**

**Moment of resistance:**

> **M_u = 0.87 f_y A_st (d − 0.42 x_u)**  — taking moments about the compression force
> **M_u = 0.36 f_ck b x_u (d − 0.42 x_u)**  — taking moments about the tension steel

Both give the same answer for a balanced or under-reinforced section, and using the **first** is safer in practice because it depends on the steel, whose yielding is the assumed failure mode.

**The limiting neutral axis depth** comes from assumption 6 — the requirement that the steel has yielded and strained beyond yield before the concrete crushes:

| Steel | **x_u,max / d** |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** |

The value **falls as the steel grade rises**, because higher-strength steel has a larger yield strain, so the neutral axis must be higher for that strain to be reached before the concrete's 0.0035 is exhausted.

**Limiting moment of resistance**, obtained by substituting x_u,max:

> **M_u,lim = 0.36 f_ck b d² (x_u,max/d)(1 − 0.42 x_u,max/d)**

which evaluates to approximately:

| Steel | M_u,lim |
|---|---|
| Fe 250 | **0.148 f_ck b d²** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.138 f_ck b d²** |
| Fe 500 | **0.133 f_ck b d²** |

**M_u,lim = 0.138 f_ck b d² for Fe 415** is the single most-used number in RCC design: it is the maximum moment a singly reinforced section of those dimensions can carry, and exceeding it means either a deeper section or compression steel.

sections.heading: Under-reinforced, balanced and over-reinforced sections
sections.body:
This is the most examined concept in reinforced concrete, and the reasoning matters more than the definitions.

| Section | Condition | Fails by | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Under-reinforced** | **x_u < x_u,max** | **Steel yields first**, then concrete crushes | **Ductile** — large deflection and wide cracks give **warning**; failure is gradual |
| **Balanced** | x_u = x_u,max | Steel yields and concrete crushes **simultaneously** | The theoretical boundary |
| **Over-reinforced** | **x_u > x_u,max** | **Concrete crushes first**, steel has not yielded | **Brittle** — **sudden, explosive**, no warning |

**Why codes require under-reinforced design.** It is not because an under-reinforced section is stronger — an over-reinforced one may carry more load. It is because of **how it fails**:

| Under-reinforced failure | Over-reinforced failure |
|---|---|
| Steel yields, deflection grows visibly | Concrete crushes at the top |
| **Cracks widen and are visible** | Little cracking beforehand |
| **Warning is given**, evacuation possible | **No warning** |
| Energy is absorbed — valuable in an **earthquake** | Little energy absorbed |
| Moment can **redistribute** to adjacent members | No redistribution |

The last two rows matter enormously in Nepal. A structure surviving an earthquake does so by **deforming inelastically and absorbing energy**, which requires ductility at every hinge; and moment redistribution in a continuous frame depends on the first-yielding section continuing to carry its moment while others take up the excess. **Both are lost in an over-reinforced section.**

This is why IS 456 does **not permit** a section with x_u > x_u,max: the code does not merely discourage it, it makes it inadmissible, and a section whose steel exceeds the limit must be redesigned as a **doubly reinforced** section or made deeper.

**A useful check.** For a given b and d, compare the applied M_u with M_u,lim:

| Condition | Action |
|---|---|
| **M_u < M_u,lim** | **Singly reinforced** section is adequate — solve for A_st |
| M_u ≈ M_u,lim | Balanced; at the economic limit |
| **M_u > M_u,lim** | Increase d, or provide **compression steel** (doubly reinforced) |

**Doubly reinforced sections.** Compression steel is provided when the section depth is **restricted** — by headroom, by architectural requirement, or to match adjacent members — and M_u exceeds M_u,lim.

> **M_u = M_u,lim + (f_sc − 0.446 f_ck) A_sc (d − d′)**

Compression steel brings two further benefits beyond capacity:

- It **reduces long-term deflection**, by resisting the **creep** of the compression concrete.
- It **improves ductility**, by confining the compression zone.

It must be **restrained by closely spaced ties**, or it will buckle outward and spall the cover — which is why compression steel without adequate links is worse than none.

**Minimum and maximum steel (IS 456 cl. 26.5.1):**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum tension steel in a beam** | **A_st/(bd) = 0.85/f_y** — about **0.205%** for Fe 415 |
| **Maximum tension steel** | **0.04 bD** (4%) |
| **Minimum in a slab** | **0.12%** of gross area (HYSD), 0.15% (mild steel) |
| Side face steel (beams deeper than 750 mm) | 0.1% of the web area |

**Why a minimum exists.** An unreinforced or very lightly reinforced section can carry a moment while uncracked — the concrete's own tensile strength suffices. But the **moment at which it cracks may exceed the moment its steel can carry**, so the instant a crack forms the section fails suddenly and completely. The minimum steel ensures the section can carry **more after cracking than the moment that caused the crack**, so failure remains ductile. That is the whole reason, and it is a favourite conceptual question.

**The maximum exists** for practical reasons: beyond about 4% the bars cannot be placed and compacted around, and the section becomes over-reinforced in any case.

sections.heading: Bond, anchorage and development length
sections.body:
**Bond** is what makes reinforced concrete possible: the transfer of force between steel and concrete along the bar surface, so that the two act as one material.

| Bond mechanism | Source |
|---|---|
| **Adhesion** | Chemical and physical grip of paste to steel |
| **Friction** | Enhanced by shrinkage of concrete onto the bar |
| **Mechanical interlock** | The **ribs of a deformed bar** bearing on concrete |

A **plain mild steel bar** relies on adhesion and friction alone, which is why it needs **hooks and bends** at its ends. A **deformed (HYSD/TMT) bar** develops most of its bond by mechanical interlock, which is why its permissible bond stress is **60% higher** and why hooks are usually unnecessary.

**Development length** is the length of bar needed to develop its full design stress by bond:

> **L_d = φ σ_s / (4 τ_bd)**

with φ the bar diameter, σ_s = **0.87 f_y** at the limit state, and τ_bd the design bond stress.

The **4** in the denominator is worth understanding: it comes from equating the bar force (πφ²/4)σ_s to the bond force (πφ L_d)τ_bd — the ratio of the bar's **area to its perimeter** is φ/4.

**Design bond stress τ_bd (IS 456 cl. 26.2.1.1)** for plain bars in tension:

| Grade | M20 | M25 | M30 | M35 | M40+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| τ_bd (N/mm²) | **1.2** | 1.4 | 1.5 | 1.7 | 1.9 |

with two increases:

> **× 1.6 for DEFORMED bars**
> **× 1.25 for bars in COMPRESSION**

So for **Fe 415 deformed bars in M20 concrete**:

> L_d = φ × (0.87 × 415) / (4 × 1.2 × 1.6) = φ × 361/7.68 ≈ **47 φ**

The familiar rule of thumb **L_d ≈ 47φ** for Fe 415 in M20, and about **56φ** for Fe 500 in M20. It **decreases with higher concrete grade** (better bond) and **increases with higher steel grade** (more force to develop).

**Where development length must be provided:**

| Location | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **At a simple support** | The bar must extend L_d/3 beyond the centre of support, or be anchored |
| **At a point of maximum stress** | Full L_d each side |
| **Where bars are curtailed** | The continuing bars must develop the remaining moment |
| **At a lap** | Lap length ≥ **L_d or 30φ**, whichever is greater (tension) |
| Compression lap | ≥ L_d in compression or 24φ |

**Lap positions matter.** Laps should be **staggered**, with not more than half the bars lapped at one section, and should be placed where the **stress is low** — near mid-span for top bars, near the support for bottom bars. Lapping all bars at the point of maximum moment creates a plane of weakness precisely where it can least be afforded.

**Anchorage by hooks and bends.** Where straight length is insufficient, the anchorage value is:

| Detail | Anchorage value |
|---|---|
| **Standard 90° bend** | **8φ** per bend (maximum 24φ) |
| **Standard U-hook (180°)** | **16φ** |

So a hook can substitute for a substantial part of L_d — which is how bars are anchored into a narrow column or a shallow support.

**Checking bond at a support.** IS 456 requires, at a simply supported end:

> **L_d ≤ M_u/V_u + L_0**

where L_0 is the anchorage beyond the centre of support. This is the **flexural bond** check, and failing it means the bar is being asked to develop stress faster than bond can transfer it — the remedy being smaller-diameter bars (more perimeter for the same area) rather than more steel.

That last point is worth stating generally: **for a given area of steel, smaller bars give more bond surface**. Four 12 mm bars have the same area as one 24 mm bar but twice the perimeter, hence twice the bond capacity and better crack control. It is why heavily loaded beams use several moderate bars rather than a few large ones.

**Curtailment of reinforcement.** Bars may be stopped where they are no longer needed for moment, but IS 456 requires them to continue a further **d or 12φ**, whichever is greater, beyond the theoretical cut-off — because the moment diagram is not exact, the shear at that point increases the steel stress, and a bar stopped abruptly in a tension zone creates a stress concentration. Curtailment points are conveniently taken at the **points of contraflexure**, which is one of the practical reasons for locating them.

sections.heading: Slabs
sections.body:
**One-way or two-way** — decided by the aspect ratio:

> **L_y/L_x > 2** → **one-way** (bends in one direction only)
> **L_y/L_x ≤ 2** → **two-way** (bends in both)

In a **one-way** slab the **main steel runs along the SHORT span** and **distribution steel** along the long span. The distribution steel is not structural in the same sense — it distributes concentrated loads, resists shrinkage and temperature effects, and holds the main bars in position — and is provided at the minimum percentage (**0.12% of gross area** for HYSD).

In a **two-way** slab both directions carry load, and the **short span carries the greater share** — because for the same deflection at the centre, the stiffer (shorter) direction must take more load. The design moments come from **IS 456 Annex D** tables, which give coefficients for nine cases of edge restraint.

**Why a slab spanning more than 2:1 is treated as one-way** is a matter of proportion rather than a sharp physical change: at a ratio of 2 the long span carries only about 6% of the load, so ignoring it and providing minimum steel in that direction is both simpler and safe.

**Design procedure for a one-way slab:**

1. **Assume a depth** from the span/depth ratio (IS 456: **20 for simply supported, 26 for continuous**, modified for the steel percentage) — the depth is fixed by **deflection**, not by moment, in almost every slab.
2. Compute loads: self weight + finishes + imposed, factored by 1.5.
3. Find M_u and V_u for a **1 m wide strip**.
4. Design for flexure, treating it as a rectangular beam of b = 1000 mm.
5. Check the **shear** — rarely governs in a slab, and shear reinforcement is generally avoided by increasing the depth.
6. Provide **distribution steel**, check **spacing** and **development length**.

**Spacing limits (IS 456 cl. 26.3.3):**

| Steel | Maximum spacing |
|---|---|
| **Main steel** | **3 d** or **300 mm**, whichever is less |
| **Distribution steel** | **5 d** or **450 mm**, whichever is less |

Minimum spacing must allow the aggregate to pass — generally the greater of the bar diameter and the maximum aggregate size plus 5 mm.

**Types of slab:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **One-way** | Supported on two opposite edges |
| **Two-way** | Supported on all four edges |
| **Flat slab** | Supported **directly on columns**, no beams — with **drops** and **column heads/capitals** to resist punching shear |
| **Ribbed / waffle** | Voids reduce dead weight; long spans |
| **Continuous** | Over several spans; uses IS 456 moment coefficients |
| **Cantilever** | Balconies, chajjas; span/depth **7** |
| Circular, flat plate | — |

The **flat slab** is worth understanding because its critical check is different: with no beams, the slab must resist **punching shear** around each column, which is why **drop panels** and **column capitals** exist — both simply increase the punching perimeter and the effective depth locally.

**Corner reinforcement in a two-way slab** is a detail that questions ask about. At a corner where two **discontinuous (simply supported) edges** meet, the slab tends to **lift**, and torsional moments develop. IS 456 therefore requires **torsion reinforcement** at such corners: mesh in **both directions, top and bottom**, over a length of **one fifth of the shorter span**, with area equal to **three quarters** of the maximum mid-span steel. Where one edge is continuous the requirement halves; where both are continuous none is needed.

**Slab detailing points**, each a common site error:

| Point | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Main steel in the SHORT direction, and placed LOWEST** | It needs the greatest effective depth |
| **Top steel over supports** in a continuous slab | Hogging moment |
| **Cover blocks under the bottom mesh** | Cover is meaningless without them |
| **Chairs supporting the top mesh** | Otherwise it is trodden down to mid-depth |
| Alternate bars **cranked or curtailed**, not all | Retain steel where moment persists |

The **chairs** point deserves emphasis: top reinforcement over a continuous support carries the hogging moment and depends entirely on being **near the top surface**. Walked down to mid-depth during concreting, it does almost nothing — and the resulting crack over the support appears within months.

formulas.label: Stress block constants
formulas.expression: C = 0.36 f_ck b x_u, with its centroid 0.42 x_u from the extreme compression fibre
formulas.note: From the parabolic-rectangular block. Maximum concrete strain 0.0035; maximum stress 0.446 f_ck.

formulas.label: Neutral axis depth and moment of resistance
formulas.note: Equivalently M_u = 0.36 f_ck b x_u (d − 0.42 x_u).

formulas.label: Limiting neutral axis and moment
formulas.note: Falls as steel grade rises, because a higher yield strain must be reached before concrete crushes.

formulas.label: Doubly reinforced section
formulas.note: Used when depth is restricted. Also reduces creep deflection and improves ductility; needs close ties.

formulas.label: Minimum and maximum steel
formulas.expression: beam minimum A_st/bd = 0.85/f_y (≈0.205% for Fe415) ;  maximum 0.04bD ;  slab minimum 0.12%
formulas.note: The minimum ensures the section carries more after cracking than the moment that cracked it.

formulas.label: Development length
formulas.expression: L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd),  σ_s = 0.87 f_y ;   τ_bd = 1.2 (M20), × 1.6 deformed, × 1.25 compression
formulas.note: ≈ 47φ for Fe 415 in M20. Falls with higher concrete grade, rises with higher steel grade.

formulas.label: Anchorage values
formulas.expression: standard 90° bend = 8φ per bend (max 24φ) ;   standard U-hook = 16φ
formulas.note: Lap length ≥ L_d or 30φ in tension. Stagger laps and place them where stress is low.

formulas.label: Flexural bond check at a support
formulas.note: Failing it calls for SMALLER bars (more perimeter per unit area), not more steel.

formulas.label: Slab classification and spacing
formulas.expression: L_y/L_x > 2 one-way, ≤ 2 two-way ;  main steel spacing ≤ 3d or 300 mm; distribution ≤ 5d or 450 mm
formulas.note: In a one-way slab the main steel runs along the SHORT span, placed lowest.

formulas.label: Corner torsion steel in a two-way slab
formulas.expression: Both edges discontinuous: mesh both ways top and bottom over L_x/5, area = 0.75 × maximum mid-span steel
formulas.note: Halved if one edge is continuous; not required if both are continuous.
